turns.prompt_text: I heard a long time ago that human beings are striped like zebras but kind of in a different way On our fronts we have an upside down u-shape pattern and in our backs we have an upside down v-shaped pattern And through some kind of specific lens or infrared light or some kind of electrical optical equipment I think if I recalled correctly that it has to be through a microscope though
turns.response_html:
You're thinking of Blaschko's lines. It is a really interesting concept, and you have some of the details almost perfectly correct, but there is a very common misconception about how they can be seen.

Here is the breakdown of what is actually going on:

The Pattern is Real

You are spot-on about the shapes. Blaschko's lines are believed to trace the migration paths of embryonic cells as a human fetus develops.

  • On the back: They form a V-shape.
  • On the chest/stomach: They form an S-shape.
  • On the chest to upper arm: They form an inverted U-shape.
  • On the limbs: They run mostly straight up and down.

The "Invisible" Myth

The part about seeing them under a microscope, UV light, or with special lenses is a very popular internet rumor, but it isn't true.

Under normal circumstances, these lines are completely invisible. You cannot shine a blacklight on a typical person and see them glowing like a zebra. They aren't a hidden pigment; they are just a map of how skin cells expanded.

So how do we know they exist? We can only see Blaschko's lines when someone has specific, often rare, skin conditions. For example, if someone has chimerism (where they possess two distinct sets of DNA) or certain genetic mutations that affect pigmentation, the differently colored skin cells will follow these exact developmental pathways.

When these conditions occur, the lines become visible to the naked eye as distinct streaks, swirls, or patches of lighter or darker skin. The German dermatologist Alfred Blaschko first mapped these patterns in 1901 by studying over 140 patients with these specific skin conditions.

turns.prompt_text: What about stretch marks like from working out you develop these purplish stretch marks especially on my upper arms around the bicep area and upper thighs
turns.response_html:
What you are describing are stretch marks, which are medically known as striae distensae. While Blaschko's lines are formed by cell migration during fetal development, stretch marks are entirely mechanical—they happen in real-time when your body grows faster than your skin can comfortably stretch.

They are incredibly common from lifting weights, particularly during periods of rapid muscle hypertrophy (growth).

Why Are They Purple?

Your skin consists of three main layers: the epidermis (outer layer), the dermis (middle layer), and the hypodermis (deepest layer).

When you build muscle quickly—like in your biceps, chest, or thighs—the skin is forced to expand rapidly. If the skin is stretched beyond its elastic limit, the connective fibers in the dermis (collagen and elastin) can actually tear.

The purplish or red color you are seeing (called striae rubrae) is literally the deeper layers of skin and the blood vessels showing through those microscopic tears in the dermis. Because they are fresh, they are often inflamed and filled with blood flow, giving them that vibrant purple or angry red color.

Will They Stay That Color?

No. Over time (usually months to a year), the blood vessels will narrow, the inflammation will die down, and the tears will heal with scar tissue.

When this happens, they fade into a silvery, pale, or white color, known as striae albae. They will look more like slight, glossy indentations in the skin rather than dark lines.

How They Differ from Blaschko's Lines

Stretch marks don't follow the embryonic pathways of Blaschko's lines. Instead, they form perpendicular to Langer's lines (also called cleavage lines). Langer's lines represent the natural orientation of collagen fibers in the dermis.

When your bicep grows, the muscle pushes outward, and the skin tears at right angles to the direction of the physical tension. That's why bicep stretch marks usually run somewhat horizontally or diagonally across the arm, near the armpit—they are simply tearing where the skin is being pulled the tightest.

turns.prompt_text: Somebody told me a while ago that dishwashers are very water and energy efficient compared to hand washing dishes and that you should always use it rather than trying to hand wash dishes I wonder if there's a way to hand wash dishes that is comparably efficient, namely if you use a very little amount of water or if you create a tub of water and reuse it They also said that you should leave food and stuff all in the dishes because the dishwasher uses that to help clean So if you rinse your dishes off too well they can hinder the dishwashing process
turns.response_html:
Whoever told you that was absolutely correct on both counts. Modern dishwashers are essentially highly optimized water-recycling robots, and they actually need your dishes to be dirty to work properly.

Here is a breakdown of why hand washing struggles to compete, and why pre-rinsing is a bad idea.

Can Hand Washing Compete?

If you leave the tap running while you wash and rinse, hand washing a full load of dishes can use upwards of 20 to 27 gallons of water. An Energy Star-certified dishwasher uses only 3 to 4 gallons for that exact same load.

You mentioned using a tub of water. This is known as the two-basin method (one tub of hot soapy water for washing, one tub of clean water for rinsing), and it is definitely the most efficient way to hand wash.

While the two-basin method drastically reduces water usage (bringing it closer to 5–10 gallons), the dishwasher still wins out on two major fronts:

  1. Water Recycling: A dishwasher doesn't constantly draw fresh water. It fills the bottom tub with a small amount of water, heats it, and aggressively pumps that exact same water through the spray arms repeatedly before draining it and drawing a tiny bit more for the final rinse.
  2. Energy Efficiency: Heating water accounts for most of the energy used in dishwashing. Your home's water heater has to heat the water and send it all the way through the pipes to your sink, losing heat along the way. A dishwasher pulls in warm water and uses a localized, internal heating element to boost the temperature, which is far more efficient.

Why You Shouldn't Pre-Rinse

The advice to leave food on your plates sounds counterintuitive, but it comes down to how modern detergents and dishwasher sensors are engineered.

1. Detergent Enzymes Need a Job

Modern dishwasher detergents don't rely on harsh phosphates anymore; they use enzymes designed specifically to attack proteins and starches. These enzymes need food particles to latch onto and break down. If you pre-rinse your dishes until they look clean, the enzymes have nothing to attack. Instead, the highly alkaline detergent can end up attacking the dishes themselves, which is what causes glassware to become cloudy and permanently etched over time.

2. The Turbidity Sensor

Almost all modern dishwashers have a component called a turbidity sensor (or soil sensor) located near the drain pump.

During the initial pre-wash cycle, the machine sprays the dishes and measures how cloudy (turbid) the water gets as it pools at the bottom.

  • If the water is very dirty: The sensor tells the machine to run a longer, hotter, more aggressive wash cycle.
  • If the water is relatively clear: The sensor assumes the dishes are already clean and defaults to a shorter, cooler, lighter cycle to save water and energy.

If you thoroughly pre-rinse your dishes, the sensor will test the water, think the dishes are clean, and run a weak cycle. Any stubborn, sticky bits of food left over simply won't get enough heat and water pressure to be removed.

The golden rule: Scrape, don't rinse. Scrape the large chunks of food (like bones, fruit pits, or heavy scraps) into the trash so they don't clog the machine's filter, but leave the sauce smears, grease, and sticky residues right where they are.

turns.prompt_text: So once I'm done eating on my plate I don't even rinse it a little bit I just put it straight into the dishwasher What if there is stuff that looks pretty hard to remove? Should I just try to scrape it quick but leave it on once I scrape it? What if right before I start the dishwasher? I just spray ranch dressing and ketchup all over it real quick
turns.response_html:
Exactly. You want to clear the debris, but keep the grime.

Here is how you should handle those specific scenarios:

The "Scrape, Don't Rinse" Rule

If you have a solid chunk of food—like a piece of meat, a large clump of rice, or half a roasted carrot—scrape that into the trash. Your dishwasher is a washing machine, not a garbage disposal. If you leave large chunks, they will just get trapped in the filter at the bottom of the tub and eventually start to smell.

But once the 3D chunks are gone, stop. Do not run it under the faucet. The smear of grease, the sticky sauce residue, and the wet crumbs should all go straight into the machine.

What About Hard-to-Remove Stuff?

For 95% of your meals, the dishwasher's heat, water pressure, and chemical enzymes are more than enough to obliterate whatever is stuck on there.

There are only two main exceptions where you might need to intervene:

  1. Baked-on, carbonized food: If you completely scorched a pan and it has a layer of black, burnt carbon glued to the bottom, the dishwasher will struggle. That requires physical soaking and scrubbing.
  2. Dried-on proteins/starches: If you leave a bowl coated in oatmeal or egg yolk sitting on the counter for two days until it turns into cement, the dishwasher might not get it all.

If it's just normal, sticky food from a meal you just ate, trust the machine and let the enzymes do their job.

The Ketchup and Ranch "Hack"

If you spray ketchup and ranch all over your dishes right before starting the machine, you will successfully trick the turbidity sensor, but it will backfire on you.

When the sensor detects all those fresh condiments swirling around in the pre-wash water, its programming will scream, "These dishes are incredibly filthy!" It will immediately abandon its energy-saving protocols and trigger the longest, hottest, and most water-heavy cycle available in its system.

The dishes will come out clean, but you will have completely defeated the water- and energy-efficiency benefits of the machine—and you'll be wasting perfectly good ketchup and ranch in the process. Just let the natural food residue left over from your meal do the work!
